section_summary: This section covers internal political tensions, civil-military conflict, and diplomatic developments in Japan between late January and late February 1932 following the Manchurian crisis and the outbreak of hostilities in Shanghai. It documents the dissolution of the 60th Diet session, the Seiyukai Party's sweeping victory in the February 20 general election, and the growing influence of radical military factions advocating a national socialist or military dictatorship. Reports from U.S. diplomats in Tokyo, Geneva, Peiping, and Shanghai analyze the erosion of parliamentary governance, economic strains, rising social unrest, and confidential Japanese peace soundings through League of Nations contacts.

subfiles.about: Assessment of civil-military rivalry, military dominance over the Foreign Office, and key army leaders shaping Manchurian policy.
subfiles.summary: Despatch reviews military-civilian conflict between General Minami and Foreign Minister Shidehara over Manchuria, profiling army officers including rising Araki, concluding the Foreign Office was subordinated to the assertive Kwantung Army.
subfiles.title: Political and Military Influences on Japanese Foreign Policy (Pages 12-14)

subfiles.about: Reuter dispatch on the dissolution of the Japanese Diet and Foreign Minister Yoshizawa's speech on Manchurian policy.
subfiles.summary: Telegram relays plans to dissolve the Diet for a Seiyukai majority bid; Foreign Minister Yoshizawa called Manchuria key to Far East peace, denied territorial designs, backed the Open Door, and welcomed Soviet neutrality.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 105 from Peiping regarding Diet Dissolution and Foreign Minister's Speech

subfiles.about: Reporting the formal dissolution of the Imperial Diet and the scheduling of general elections.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports that the Diet was dissolved immediately following ministerial policy speeches by the Prime Minister, Foreign Minister, and Finance Minister. A general election is expected for February 20. The Foreign Minister's address focused on Manchuria and the upcoming Geneva Arms Conference without referencing American immigration laws.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 19 from Tokyo Reporting Dissolution of the Diet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note for Despatch No. 460 regarding the Sakurada Gate assassination attempt on Emperor Hirohito.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 460 on the assassination attempt against Emperor Hirohito by Lee Bong-chang and the Cabinet's response.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 460 on Attempt Against Emperor Hirohito

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note for Despatch No. 458 regarding the Chinchow situation and the Secretary of State's remarks.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 458 on Chinchow's political situation and reaction to Stimson's November 27 remarks.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 458 on Chinchow Political Situation

subfiles.about: Fragmentary report analyzing domestic Japanese criticism of Shidehara regarding military secrets and the advance on Chinchow.
subfiles.summary: Excerpt describes attacks on Shidehara and the Chief of Staff over an alleged Chinchow agreement, accusing Shidehara of leaking secrets to Ambassador Forbes and infringing imperial command, amid press outrage over American inquiries.
subfiles.title: Report Excerpt on Chinchow Advance and Accusations against Shidehara

subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Stimson's memo on Ambassador Claudel's view that Japan's domestic situation was highly precarious and could spark revolution.

subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr., Under Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Castle's memo citing the Nanking incident as administrative breakdown, with Kabayama discussing Japan's constitutional governing difficulties.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Castle Memorandum on Talk with Count Kabayama

subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Wilson telegram on the possibility the Inukai-Yoshizawa Cabinet could be overthrown by a military-led cabinet.

subfiles.from: Richard P. Butrick, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Butrick's memo on a Whaley-Eaton Foreign Letter about Japanese political conditions.

subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Hornbeck's memo forwarding Chester Rowell's observations on general internal conditions in Japan.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Hornbeck Memorandum on Chester Rowell's Observations

subfiles.about: Analysis of the dissolution of the Diet, party maneuvers, and the political platforms for the February 1932 election.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes details the imperial dissolution of the 60th Diet session and the calling of a general election for February 20, 1932. He contrasts the economic programs of the Seiyukai (bond issues, gold embargo, inflation) and Minseito (deflation, retrenchment, gold standard). The despatch explains how the Inukai government dissolved the Lower House before debate could proceed and analyzes the political fallout of the Sakurada Gate incident and the Adachi schism.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 471: Dissolution of the Diet and Forthcoming General Election

subfiles.about: Confidential analysis of domestic instability, radical young army officer sentiment, and the danger of a military coup d'état.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports pervasive anxiety in Japan concerning potential military dictatorship or violent domestic upheavals. He recounts an unpublicized November incident in which an armed junior officer confronted Chief of Staff Kanaya over perceived weakness in Manchuria without facing punishment. The report discusses Araki's influence over the young officers, military hostility toward party politicians and zaibatsu capitalists like Mitsui and Mitsubishi, rural economic distress, and growing social unrest.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 472: Domestic Political Situation and Military Ascendancy

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on War Minister Araki's perceived conservatism among his military followers.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a telegram: the War Minister acted conservatively enough that radical followers doubted his backing of extreme goals.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 65 on War Minister's Policies

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note regarding Belgian Ambassador Bassompierre's appraisal of the Manchurian crisis.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a despatch on Baron Bassompierre's views, the Belgian Ambassador, regarding the Manchurian conflict.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch on Baron Bassompierre's Views

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on difficulties facing conservative Japanese elements in opposing government war policies.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a telegram: Forbes notes Japanese conservatives' difficulty opposing military policy without being branded unpatriotic.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 70 on Conservative Opposition

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Yosuke Matsuoka's statement regarding the Shanghai conflict.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a telegram quoting Matsuoka's remark that Japan wanted an honorable exit from Shanghai but saw none.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram on Matsuoka's Statement on Shanghai

subfiles.about: Report on Japanese military operations in Shanghai and a private interview with Yosuke Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: Johnson reports minimal Japanese progress in Shanghai despite intense attacks; Matsuoka admitted Japan wanted an honorable exit but couldn't accept defeat or withdraw before Chinese resistance.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Shanghai on Military Operations and Talk with Matsuoka

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note stating Japan rejects mediation in Shanghai due to national prestige.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a telegram: Japan considers its military prestige at stake in Shanghai and will refuse outside mediation.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram on Japanese Rejection of Mediation

subfiles.about: Initial returns indicating a record Seiyukai parliamentary election victory.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports Seiyukai's landslide 304-147 election win over Minseito, the largest majority in Japanese history, seen as desire for change amid muted excitement over China.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 75 Reporting Seiyukai General Election Victory

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on rumors of an impending change in the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a telegram on confidential reports of a grave situation and rumors of imminent cabinet reorganization.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 76 on Rumored Government Changes

subfiles.about: Rumors of a cabinet crisis, troop dispatches to Shanghai, and wartime press censorship.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports persistent coalition-cabinet rumors despite the Seiyukai win, the War Office sending more divisions to Shanghai disrupting U.S. officers' War College assignments, and strict press censorship hampering news gathering.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 76 on Political Instability and Shanghai Reinforcements

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on diplomat Naotake Sato's initiative to end Shanghai hostilities.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Wilson telegram: Sato would urge Japan to halt hostilities and restore cooperation with Western powers.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Wilson Telegram on Sato Peace Initiative

subfiles.about: Confidential Geneva talks between Naotake Sato and American delegates Gibson and Davis on ending Shanghai fighting under the Nine Power Treaty.
subfiles.summary: Wilson reports Sato's Geneva talk with Gibson and Davis over runaway Shanghai operations threatening Manchuria, planning to urge Japan take diplomatic initiative with U.S./British help, suggesting the Nine Power Treaty framework before the League Assembly meets.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 35 from Geneva on Sato Peace Soundings

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on intense Japanese public excitement over military troop deployments.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a telegram on nationalist demonstrations accompanying reinforcements dispatched to China.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 78 on Troop Departures

subfiles.about: Atmosphere of war excitement in Tokyo, troop departures, and diplomatic forecasts of a military premier.
subfiles.summary: Forbes describes crowds cheering departing troops at Tokyo stations, requiring heavy police escort for the Ambassador, with British and Italian envoys anticipating a cabinet reorganization under a military premier.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 78 on Nationalist Excitement and Forecast of Military Premier

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on Japanese economic desperation from Chinese boycotts leading to aggressive measures at Shanghai.
subfiles.from: Joseph E. Jacobs, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Jacobs memo: the Chinese boycott's effects drove Japan to frantic, disproportionate actions at Shanghai.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Jacobs Memorandum on Boycott and Shanghai Action

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note regarding Japanese Ambassador Debuchi's satisfaction with the Seiyukai election victory.
subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr., Under Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Castle memo: Japan's Ambassador expressed relief the Seiyukai secured a definitive Diet majority.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Castle Memorandum on Talk with Japanese Ambassador

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on Ambassador Matsudaira's view against linking Shanghai to the Manchurian issue.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Wilson telegram: Matsudaira warned against combining the Shanghai conflict with Manchurian affairs amid agitated opinion.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Wilson Telegram on Matsuodaira's Views

subfiles.about: Confidential discussion between Norman Davis and Ambassador Matsudaira regarding diplomatic steps for a Shanghai armistice.
subfiles.summary: Wilson recounts Davis-Matsudaira dinner talk: Matsudaira said Japan couldn't seek armistice directly without appearing weak, urging interested powers initiate peace proposals while deferring Manchuria to the Lytton Commission, agreeing action was urgently needed before opinion hardened.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 38 from Geneva on Davis-Matsudaira Discussions

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note on civil-military discord over creating an independent Manchurian state.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a telegram on policy rifts between the army clique favoring Manchurian independence and opposed civilian ministers.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 81 on Civil-Military Rift on Manchuria

subfiles.about: Conversation with Foreign Minister Yoshizawa concerning the proposed independent Manchurian state and cabinet resistance.
subfiles.summary: Forbes recounts questioning Yoshizawa regarding plans for an independent Manchurian regime, noting implications for Chinese integrity, debts, and internal laws. Yoshizawa declined to define the government's stance, reinforcing widespread reports of a policy split between junior military officers promoting Manchurian independence and civilian ministers who oppose it.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 81 on Foreign Minister's Views on Manchurian Independence

subfiles.about: Detailed analysis of military radicalism, reactionary terror, fascist ideological trends, and the prospect of a military dictatorship.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville (for Ambassador Forbes), Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The despatch assesses pervasive expectations of fundamental political upheaval driven by radical army officers and reactionary groups amidst acute agrarian and economic crisis. It documents a growing atmosphere of terror, highlighted by the assassination of former Finance Minister Inouye and intimidation directed at Dr. Nitobe for criticizing the military clique. The report analyzes ideological drift among proletarian parties toward national socialism and discusses Genro Saionji's maneuverings to construct a non-party coalition under Baron Hiranuma to stave off an outright coup.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 512: Potential Political Upheaval and Rise of Fascism in Japan

subfiles.about: Comprehensive statistical and political review of the February 20, 1932 general election and the Seiyukai landslide.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville (for Ambassador Forbes), Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Neville provides a comprehensive analysis of the February 20, 1932 general election, where the Seiyukai won an unprecedented 304 seats against the Minseito's 147. The victory is attributed to administrative control over police and voting machinery, corporate campaign contributions following the gold embargo, nationalist rallying behind the military, and public exhaustion with Minseito austerity. The report examines historical voting data since 1915, the collapse of proletarian representation, press warnings about the decline of parliamentary prestige, and the election of Korea-born candidate Park Chun-geum.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 509: Comprehensive Report on the General Election of February 20, 1932

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Ambassador Forbes's clarification regarding reliance on Japan's word.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a despatch clarifying Forbes's earlier statement that Japan's word could no longer be relied on.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch Clarifying Ambassador Forbes's Statement

subfiles.about: Confidential letter detailing last-minute mail dispatches via SS President Wilson and diplomatic proposals brought by Counselor Neville.
subfiles.summary: Forbes explains rushing earlier correspondence onto a departing steamship, beginning to address details of Counselor Neville's return with an official Japanese proposition.
subfiles.title: Confidential Despatch Fragment on Japanese Propositions
